Taxco lies in the mountainous part of Guerrero State and is known for its silver craftsmanship. In the colonial center, streets lead to squares, workshops and jewelry shops. The town's hillside buildings add views of neighboring quarters to the experience of discovering the work of local artisans.

One of its main landmarks is the Baroque Church of Santa Prisca. Nearby is the Zócalo, with restaurants and silver shops. Taxco combines architecture with a look at traditional craftsmanship: historic facades and contemporary jewelry reveal different sides of a town long associated with working silver.

Tayrona lies on Colombia's Caribbean coast near Santa Marta. Tropical vegetation reaches the sea, and forest trails connect different stretches of coastline. The natural landscape is closely tied to the history of the region's Indigenous cultures, making a visit rewarding beyond the beaches alone.

One walking route leads from the Cañaveral sector through Arrecifes to Cabo San Juan. Along the way, the scenery alternates between forest and open coastal views. Each beach offers a different experience of the park: in one area the rocks and water draw your attention, while elsewhere shaded paths and coastal vegetation are the highlights.

### Tegucigalpa — the capital of Honduras

Set in a bowl-shaped valley around 1,000 meters above sea level, the city was founded in 1524 by Spanish conquistadors. An Indigenous (Aztec) settlement stood on the site of today's capital before the Spanish seized it during their conquest of what is now Honduras.

Nearby is a silver mine that has been worked since the 16th century. The capital's name, Tegucigalpa, is associated with the expression "Silver Mountain." The city occupies a scenic position at the foot of and along the slopes of Mount El Picacho. Stone bridges, including one dating from colonial times, connect the hilly city with districts identified as Comayagua on the plateau.

## Highlights of Tegucigalpa

### Markets — the local flavor of Tegucigalpa

Tegucigalpa has never suffered from fires or earthquakes, and much of its colonial atmosphere remains. Its markets are among the city's attractions. In addition to agricultural produce, they sell traditional handicrafts, including clay pottery, woven baskets and carved wooden sculptures.

In Tehuantepec, discovering southern Mexico begins with color. Embroidered flowers bloom across the traditional clothing of Tehuana women, while old streets lead to Santo Domingo Church and the former Dominican monastery. The town stands on the isthmus in Oaxaca State, where Zapotec culture lives on in clothing, family customs and festivals.

The historic center invites a leisurely walk with frequent stops. Visitors can study the facades, enter the church and discover the town's cultural heritage in the former monastery complex. Its 16th-century architecture recalls the colonial past, while a local guide can help reveal the much older history of the isthmus's inhabitants.

The traditional Tehuana costume deserves special attention. Bright floral embroidery on dark fabric, jewelry and its striking silhouette make it a recognizable symbol of the region. Behind the beauty of each outfit are craftsmanship, family memory and festive traditions. Watching the embroiderers at work is as absorbing as exploring the architecture: every large flower is composed of countless small stitches.

Tehuantepec is part of a travel route across the Isthmus of Oaxaca, connecting towns with different crafts and customs. It suits travelers eager to experience Mexico through its living local culture. Leave plenty of time for your walk: a stop by an old building, a conversation about embroidery and an insight into everyday life come together to create a warm, detailed impression of the town.
